title: From learning to leaderboard: How Cisco upskilled 1,200 engineers in agentic AI with AWS AI League
abstract: Cisco, like many large engineering organizations, is adopting generative and agentic AI to change how its engineers build software. The hard part is no longer access to the technology. It’s helping thousands of engineers move from watching a demo to confidently building with it. Recorded sessions and slide decks rarely close that gap. Engineers learn fastest when they build something real, see it fail, fix it, and try again. AWS designed AWS AI League for exactly that. It turns hands-on AI learning into a gamified competition, where participants customize models and build agents on AWS, get instant feedback on a live leaderboard, and compete in a game-show-style finale. Cisco is one of the clearest examples of what this looks like at scale. In 2025, Hemanth V, a Cisco software engineer, went from an internal Cisco event to being crowned the first AWS AI League Champion at AWS re:Invent 2025. In 2026, 1,200 Cisco engineers competed in an AWS AI League tournament at Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0. The winner, Nishanth Aluhonnu, earned a full event pass to AWS re:Invent 2026 in Las Vegas. In this post, we share how Cisco and AWS used Cisco Transformation Fest and AWS AI League to build a lasting culture of learning by doing. We previously covered this program in From theory to delivery: How Atos upskilled 400 engineers in agentic AI , and here we look at Cisco’s experience. We walk through Cisco’s journey, share technical lessons from the 2026 winning agent, and explain how your organization can host its own AWS AI League. What is AWS AI League? AWS AI League helps organizations build advanced AI skills through competition. Each league follows three steps: Learn – A hands-on, 2-hour workshop led by AWS experts introduces the tools and the challenge. Build – Participants experiment at their own pace and submit to a live leaderboard, with an automated evaluator giving real-time feedback after each submission. Compete – Top finalists take the stage in a live, game-show-style grand finale. Although AWS AI League offers multiple use cases, at Cisco it offered the following two challenges: Agentic AI challenge – Participants build agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. The agents move through a maze-like grid, solving challenges on the way to a treasure chest. The challenges map to real-world tasks such as handling inappropriate content, running code, retrieving information from the web, and extracting structured data. Builders can choose models for supervisor and sub-agents and add tools such as AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , and AWS Lambda Event Functions . Builders use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to apply safety controls to their agents. Model customization challenge – Participants fine-tune models in Amazon SageMaker Studio using the latest training recipes. The challenge awards points when an automated evaluator rates a participant’s customized model as more accurate and comprehensive than a reference model on the specific tasks in the competition. Finalists are scored on time efficiency, accuracy, agent planning, and token consumption efficiency. Figure 1: AWS AI League champion at AWS re:Invent 2025 Figure 2: 2026 AWS AI League winner at Cisco campus The Cisco and AWS partnership The AWS AI League story at Cisco grows out of a deep engineering partnership. Cisco and AWS bring together networking, cloud, security, and observability for shared customers including: Cisco SD-WAN , whose controller architecture runs on AWS and serves customers globally as a software as a service (SaaS) application. Cisco Meraki , Cisco Spaces , and Cisco’s IoT and smart buildings group. Cisco Cloud Control , a cloud-native, AI-powered application integrated with AWS services that brings together security, networking, observability, and collaboration. Cisco AI Defense , where Cisco’s security team uses Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker

title: Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: Serving a model from more than one AWS Region is a well-established pattern for highly available inference: when one Region runs short of GPU capacity, requests move to another. The pattern is simple to describe and hard to operate. Until now, if you served models on Amazon SageMaker AI managed endpoints, cross-Region routing was a piece you still had to build yourself. Today, we’re introducing cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. It uses a new resource, the inference router, that gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in one or more AWS Regions and AWS accounts. You register the destinations that serve a model, and your application invokes the router instead of a specific endpoint. The router keeps requests in its own Region while the local destination is healthy, shifts new requests to another registered destination when it isn’t, and returns traffic gradually after recovery. In this post, we explain how cross-Region inference routing decides where each request runs, walk through an example with one model in two Regions, and cover monitoring, limits, and what you pay. For a cross-account deployment that serves several models, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI . When one Region runs short of capacity A SageMaker AI endpoint runs in one AWS Region and one account. When autoscaling can’t add instances of the type your endpoint needs, requests throttle and time out, even when the same model has spare capacity in another Region. To use that capacity, your application must detect a struggling endpoint and switch Regions, decide which errors are safe to retry without running the model twice, move traffic back after recovery without flapping, and manage access to endpoints in other accounts. That code sits on the critical path of every request, and every team serving models across Regions maintains its own version of it. How cross-Region inference routing works Cross-Region inference routing is based on a few core ideas: You decide where your model might run – For each model, you choose which endpoints and inference components the router might use. SageMaker AI decides which destination serves each request – The router prefers its own Region and shifts new requests to another destination only when the local one can’t serve reliably. Your endpoints stay the same – You deploy endpoints as you do today, with the same models, configurations, instance pools, and autoscaling. Direct InvokeEndpoint calls keep working, and the router passes InferenceId and CustomAttributes through, as InvokeEndpoint does. You can see every decision – Each real-time response tells you which destination served the request and why. A few terms describe the pieces: Inference router – A Regional SageMaker AI resource in your account that your application invokes. Routing target – A name for one logical model on a router, such as fraud-model . A router can hold many routing targets, and each fails over independently of the others. Destination – A real-time endpoint, inference component, or asynchronous endpoint registered under a routing target, identified by its full Amazon Resource Name (ARN), which tells the router its Region and account. A routing target holds either real-time destinations, which can mix endpoints and inference components across Regions and accounts, or asynchronous endpoints only. Local destination – A destination in the router’s Region, preferred while it’s healthy. Routing reason – A value returned with each real-time response that explains where the request went and why. The Region you create the router in is its local Region. To prefer a different Region, create a router there. The router doesn’t create capacity, scale your endpoints, deploy models, or copy model artifacts and container images. Each destination must already be running in its Region. Figure 1: Each request

title: Protect agent tool calls with Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
abstract: In this post, we show how Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway keep sensitive data out of the tools your AI agents call, and out of the model context those tools feed. We add Skyflow Detect to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway as a request and response interceptor . The Skyflow interceptor de-identifies data before it reaches a tool, restores it before the agent reads the result, and replaces documents with clean copies before the agent opens them. Your agents and tools don’t change. Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace, and the interceptor is open source on GitHub. Agents act through tools, and tools move data Agents have moved from answering questions to taking action, and they take action through tools: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, SaaS APIs, document stores, and web search. Every agent tool call is a data flow. Most enterprise controls cover what goes into and comes out of the model. Far fewer cover what an agent sends to its tools or what those tools send back. That gap shows up in three ways: Sensitive data leaves through tool arguments. The model writes the arguments from everything in its context, including details the tool doesn’t need. Ask an agent about a customer, and the customer’s name, account number, or email goes straight into a query to a third-party server. That server sits outside your AWS account and your compliance scope. Sensitive data comes back in tool results. Scraped web pages, CRM records, and case notes land in the model’s context, memory, traces, and logs. This happens even when the task never needed them. Documents bypass text inspection. Document tools such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Box, and Google Drive return a signed URL, not text. A filter that inspects strings sees a link and lets it through, and the agent then opens the original file. Patching each agent doesn’t scale across teams and frameworks, and it can’t reach third-party tools. The controls need to sit where every tool call passes, so authorization, content safety, and data protection apply the same way to every agent and tool. AgentCore Gateway is that place. It fronts every tool an agent uses, whatever framework or model the agent runs on. It does more than route that traffic. With AgentCore Gateway interceptors, you can run your own code, as an AWS Lambda function, on every call that passes through it. A request interceptor sees each call before it reaches a tool, and a response interceptor sees each result before it reaches the agent. Either one can inspect the payload, rewrite it, or block the call. That makes the gateway a natural place to add data protection alongside Policy and Guardrails. This single control, attached once, covers every agent and every tool behind the gateway, without any change to agent or tool code. Example: A dispute-resolution agent at a large European bank Consider a large European bank with retail and corporate banking operations and strict data-residency obligations. Its operations teams are adopting agents to investigate card disputes. An analyst asks the agent to look into a disputed transaction. The agent searches the web for the merchant, then pulls the dispute case note from Amazon S3 to summarize it. Without protection, three things happen: The model builds the search query from everything in context. The search provider receives ‘Mateo Jackson dispute AnyCompany Electronics London’. That’s the customer’s name, sent to a third party, for a search that only needed the merchant. Scraped merchant pages bring unrelated personal data into the model’s context. The agent reads the original case note, with the customer’s full name, email, phone number, and card details. With the Skyflow interceptor on the gateway, the same workflow plays out differently: The search provider receives ‘[NAME_AJbrIud] dispute AnyCompany Electronics London’, where [NAME_AJbrIud] is a reversible vault token. What Happened to Silicon Valley?
abstract: On October 16, 2026, I delivered the second Annual Margaret Levi Lecture in Political Economy in conjunction with the AI and History conference at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. This is my original lecture as written, which incorporates material from many pieces I’ve written over the years. As delivered, I departed significantly from the script, as you can see from the embedded video below or the transcript that you can see at the link above. It’s an honor to give a lecture in Margaret Levi’s name. I’ve been asked to reflect on the changes in the political economy of Silicon Valley throughout my 40-plus year career in and about it, and I can’t imagine a better framing for my remarks than Margaret’s vision. Margaret understood that advances in our ability to work together are essential to a better future. Cooperation is the human superpower. She also asks what happens when the systems of cooperation we have constructed over time stop holding up their end of the bargain. That is very much the question that Silicon Valley is facing today. An industry that pioneered advances in collective intelligence at scale used to engender love from its customers because of the way it solved new problems in their lives. It now too often inspires fear and loathing. How did things go so wrong? The web I thought we were building in 1993 But let me start with my own history. I started my company more than 40 years ago with a $500 initial investment. We took in no venture capital, and we built a business that now generates hundreds of millions of dollars in profitable annual revenue, funded by customers who love our products and pay us for them. We got there the slow way, through steady organic growth. That is quite anathema to the rush to the top of whatever appears to be the latest hill that seems to characterize Silicon Valley today. Even when climbing that hill traps a company at a local maximum, the hope is to get to payday before the industry moves on to the next hill. My original corporate goal was stated as simply “Interesting work for interesting people.” That evolved into two principles: “Change the world by spreading the knowledge of innovators,” and “Create more value than you capture.” Those principles shaped not only my company but what I expected the internet to be. When we launched GNN , the Global Network Navigator, in 1993, it was the first web portal and the first ad-supported site on the World Wide Web, and for two years it was the place people went to find other sites. What we built was a machine for pointing you at the best of what other people had made, and then getting out of your way. Even our idea of advertising was not what you think of today. It was inspired by direct mail advertising, where you’d read articles in a print magazine or look at accompanying ads, and then you’d call an 800 number or circle a number on a “bingo card” that you’d send in to the publisher so that the advertiser could send you a brochure. I realized that the web would be a good replacement for that awkward system, that every company ought to have its own website that provided more information about its products and services. What we invented was not the “grab your attention” kind of advertising. It was all about utility, and sharing information that customers really wanted and needed. In short, it was the commercial web, which no one any longer thinks of as advertising, even though it is the most durable and useful kind. The commercial web was only a small part of what the web became. The web was the playground of amateurs, not entrepreneurs. It was a marvelous collective work of human imagination, creativity, sharing, and ultimately (though that became toxic only later), competition for attention. Our hand-curated catalog of the best websites was soon surpassed by algorithmic solutions like those provided by Google. The amount of content produced was far larger than purely human curation could manage. It was an early example of what Rich

title: This Week in AI: AI’s Next Reality Check
abstract: AI’s growing role in business is exposing challenges that new models alone can’t solve. On the latest episode of This Week in AI , we examined restrictions on autonomous agents, NVIDIA’s leadership crisis, and research into making AI systems more reliable. Agentic commerce is running into resistance Anthropic is turning Claude into a broader workplace platform. Alongside its upgraded Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 models, the company introduced Claude Meetings and Claude Sheets, Whiteboards, and Data . Anthropic also expanded its enterprise offerings with self-hosted agent infrastructure . Companies can connect agents to internal systems while keeping credentials and session histories on their own infrastructure, even though the models still run through an external provider. OpenAI is bringing more of the shopping process into ChatGPT. Its new business profiles let companies manage how customers discover them, while business agents can answer questions and recommend products. The company also introduced ChatGPT Wallet , which allows agents to make purchases without accessing customers’ actual payment card details. Users still need to review and approve these transactions before payment. Bringing business discovery and payments into ChatGPT puts OpenAI in more direct competition with search engines and online marketplaces. Airlines, banks, and retailers, however, are already restricting outside agents. United Airlines is blocking unauthorized agents from booking flights, while financial institutions and retailers, including Amazon and eBay , have imposed their own limits. Their concerns include privacy, security, and unintended purchases. An agent may be technically capable of completing a transaction but prohibited from accessing the service. Developers will need to account for those limits, while businesses that allow such transactions must establish who bears responsibility when an agent makes an unintended purchase. NVIDIA faces a test of leadership and governance NVIDIA founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following reports of personal relationships that prompted an investigation into potential national security concerns. US authorities have been investigating whether a Chinese businesswoman involved in the controversy had intelligence ties to Beijing. Those allegations remain unproven. NVIDIA’s board launched its own investigation, and longtime CFO Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent successor. NVIDIA’s influence over the AI chip market makes its leadership transition especially consequential for customers and investors. Huang led the company for 33 years and helped establish its dominant position in AI infrastructure. Now Kress and the board must maintain customer confidence while navigating the investigation. We also discussed NVIDIA’s investments in other AI companies and the circular financing arrangements that have raised concerns about how the industry measures growth. Any changes to those investments could affect companies that depend on NVIDIA for both computing infrastructure and capital. NVIDIA’s leadership transition also raises questions about succession at founder-led technology companies. After three decades with Huang at the helm, the board must show it can provide independent oversight and maintain the company’s direction through a period of uncertainty. How NVIDIA manages that transition could offer lessons for other AI companies whose identities remain closely tied to their founders. Researchers are probing why AI systems fail New research found that giving AI agents memory of previous tasks can make them perform worse than without memory when they learn the wrong lesson or apply past experiences out of context. The proposed WikiTrace system links memories to their original tasks and evidence, allowing agents to check what they’ve learned before acting. title: Claude Watermarks Your Words, and You Can’t Check Them (Yet)
abstract: I love using AI as a writing tool. But like I wrote in “ Why Does AI Write Like Yoda? ,” it’s not because AI is a good writer. In fact, it’s pretty bad at writing, and I edit absolutely everything it generates, so the end result is basically unrecognizable compared to what it created. Unfortunately, just because AI is, on average, a pretty lousy writer, that doesn’t stop people from using AI to write all sorts of things that people end up reading, and that’s how we end up with slop. That’s where watermarking comes in. If AI-written text carries a hidden signal that a machine can pick up, someone could build slop filters with it and add a little friction to mass-producing AI text and stuffing it into every nook and cranny of the internet and, maybe, manage to keep some spaces on the internet for people. (Anthropic and OpenAI give a more official reason: the EU AI Act now requires them to mark AI-generated content in a way machines can read. I don’t know how they feel about slop.) The upshot is that almost everything Claude writes now carries a hidden watermark. A slop filter needs a way to check for the watermark. And, unfortunately, for the time being, only the big AI companies and a few organizations they’ve approved can check for it. Anthropic’s support page on marking AI-generated content now reports all of its newest models, and some older ones, watermark their text on every surface where you can use Claude, worldwide. (Bruce Hopkins covered what Anthropic announced here on Radar .) Google has used a text watermark in its Gemini app since 2024, and in October OpenAI announced it’s adding one to ChatGPT and Codex text in the EU. But none of those companies lets the public check text with its detector. (Google’s synthid.com lets anyone check images, video, and audio for its watermark, including images made with ChatGPT, but it won’t let you check text from any AI lab.) I’ve read articles about watermarking, but I didn’t really know much about how it worked. So I did what any good developer would probably do: I took a shot at reasoning about it, and I came up with what I thought was a plausible way watermarking could work, based on what I know about how large language models work. And, strangely enough, it turned out I was basically right, and not because I’m some sort of amazing genius. It’s because watermarking is actually pretty straightforward, and if you know how the output part of an LLM works, you can probably design a decent watermarking system yourself. The reason I’ve got such a big interest in how models work right now is my next O’Reilly book, a deep dive into how models work called Be the Model , which we’re planning on releasing early next year. I’ve spent a lot of time over the last year thinking really hard about how to explain the internals of LLMs, and it turns out that you don’t need to understand most of the parts inside a model to see how watermarking works. All you need is the very tail end. So let’s try an experiment. I’m going to describe the relevant bits of how models work, and then, before I explain how watermarking works, I want you to take a guess and see how close you come. The only part of the model you need There’s a lot of stuff that happens inside a model. You’ve probably heard of transformer blocks, and you might know what a context window is. We all know that when you pay an API bill, you pay some number of dollars per million tokens, but we don’t always explain what a token is. title: Who Builds the Next Model?
abstract: AI is building AI At Anthropic, Claude now writes more than 80% of the code the company merges. At Google, an AI agent called AlphaEvolve found a way to make Gemini train faster. At OpenAI, an “automated research intern” now carries out research tasks under human direction. Put those together and a pattern appears. AI is starting to help build the next version of AI. Researchers call this recursive self-improvement . AI improves itself, the better version improves itself again, and the cycle repeats. The idea is old. In 1965, the mathematician I.J. Good predicted that a smart enough machine could design an even smarter one. Today we can watch it happen in small, real steps. AI went from the thing we build to something that builds with us, and now it is starting to build itself. That is the real turning point. How AI improves itself Every method follows the same simple loop. The AI tries something, checks how it did, changes something about itself, and keeps the change only if it helps. The difference between methods is what the AI is allowed to change. Here are the four levels, from simplest to most powerful. Level What it improves How it works Example What can go wrong 1. Retry Its answer Checks its own work and tries again, inside one task Reflexion, Self-Refine It sounds sure but is still wrong. 2. Rewrite Its instructions Rewrites its own prompt after seeing what failed OPRO, Promptbreeder A fix for one case breaks another. 3. Accumulate Its toolbox Saves what worked so it can reuse it later Voyager Old tricks stop working when things change. 4. Modify itself Its brain and its own code Retrains on its own best answers, or rewrites the code that runs or trains it STaR, Self-Rewarding, Absolute Zero, Darwin Godel Machine, AlphaEvolve Mistakes get baked in and can break the checks meant to catch them. It learns from its mistakes. In Reflexion , when the AI fails, it writes itself a short note about what went wrong and reads it before trying again. That simple habit lifted GPT-4’s score on a well-known coding test from 80% to 91%. But it only works when there is a clear signal, like a failing test. Google DeepMind found that when AI checks its own reasoning with no outside help, it often fails and can make things worse. It rewrites its own instructions. In Google DeepMind’s OPRO , the AI looks at its past prompts and their scores, then writes a better prompt. Its prompts beat human-written ones by up to 50% on some tasks. It builds a toolbox. Voyager plays Minecraft and saves every piece of code that worked, so it can reuse it later. Because it builds on what it already knows, it reaches goals up to 15 times faster than earlier agents. It grades itself. Meta’s Self-Rewarding Language Models judge their own answers and then learn from those judgments, with no human ratings. After three rounds, the model beat GPT-4 0613 and Claude 2 on a popular leaderboard. It teaches itself. In STaR , the AI explains its reasoning, keeps only the explanations that led to correct answers, and trains on them. It ended up matching a model about 30 times bigger. Absolute Zero goes further. The AI makes up its own practice problems, solves them, and checks the answers by running code. No human-written training examples at all. It rewrites its own code. The Darwin Godel Machine creates new versions of itself and keeps the ones that score better. Its score on a real-world coding test went from 20% to 50%. It speeds up AI training. Google’s AlphaEvolve found a faster way to do a key calculation inside Gemini, which cut Gemini’s training time by 1%. Small, but it is AI making AI cheaper to build. It does research. Sakana’s AI Scientist, whose design is now published in Nature , wrote a research paper entirely on its own that scored high enough to be accepted in blind peer review at an ICLR workshop. title: Modeling Software’s Business Impact
abstract: The following article was originally published on James Shore’s Successful Software blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. Are your teams working on the right thing? It doesn’t matter how fast they are if they’re running in the wrong direction. This is part 4 of my series on assessing AI’s impact on software development. Unlike the other essays in this series, this one isn’t really about AI at all. It’s about building the right thing. Or, more accurately, understanding the value of what you build. Because, ultimately, your ROI isn’t about how you build your software, but what you deliver, and what changes as a result. In part 1 , we looked at why assessing impact is important, and what not to do. In part 2 , we looked at how to measure AI’s impact on delivery speed. In part 3 , we considered how to measure the unintended consequences of using AI. Now, in this part, we’re examining how to model and forecast business outcomes. Finally, the epilogue puts it all together with notes you can share with your CFO. Measuring the wrong thing You’d think that modeling the value of what teams produce would be a no-brainer, but it’s surprisingly rare. It’s not particularly difficult. It’s just…organizationally complex. And there are some unavoidable compromises. Most of all, modeling value just isn’t something people think about with software development. They’ll spend months trying to fine-tune cost estimates and predictions and put hardly any thought at all into making the software more valuable . But there’s no guaranteed relationship between software cost and value. You can spend $20 million developing software that’s worthless, and $2 million developing software that transforms a business. Cost improvements are typically marginal, and difficult. Value improvements are game-changing. Focusing on value is particularly important in the AI era. If writing code is no longer a bottleneck, then what is? Early signs point to the bottleneck moving to our customers . Lee Eason, an engineering leader I spoke to recently, hypothesizes that customers have a limited ability to absorb new features. When software development was expensive, we used that cost to force prioritization. Pet projects ended up on the back burner, and the most valuable work rose to the top. (Well, sometimes. I wish it was that clean.) Now, we can produce a lot more work, but that doesn’t mean customers can absorb it. They’ve got their own work to do. Eventually, they’ll stop paying attention. We need to treat customer attention as the scarce resource it is and only ship the things that are truly valuable. Unlike the engineering bottleneck, this one’s invisible. In the old days, if we didn’t prioritize, we didn’t ship our most impactful work. In the AI era, our most impactful work could just be ignored. I’m not going to talk about how to improve value in this series, but I am going to talk about how to plan and prioritize it. Because nothing else matters if customers don’t care about your software. The attribution problem Part of the reason people measure costs is that it’s easy. Measuring value is easy, too, at the big picture level. It’s the literal bottom line. The challenge is attributing where changes to the bottom line came from. Let’s say you release a new feature and see purchases improve 10%. That’s fantastic! Chalk it up to the new release! But your VP of sales also launched a quota-retirement promotion that put the sales team into a feeding frenzy. And marketing got an important tech influencer to drive tens of thousands of people to your home page. The partnerships team stepped up too, convincing your partners to highlight their integration with your new feature in their own products. Who gets the credit for the success? Obviously, everybody contributed. But how much? Was your new feature relevant at all, or was the success due to the sales, marketing, and partner push? title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
abstract: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled. The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work. It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development. And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement. METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research. In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance. Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.” Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fal

title: The Download: inside the quest to make our minds immortal
abstract: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. What we learned when our Roundtables explored the quest to make minds immortal To preserve our sense of self, some scientists are working on ways to keep our brains going—even beyond death. In their quest for cognitive immortality, these “mind savers” are exploring everything from head transplants and brain freezing to conscious software avatars. In the latest MIT Technology Review Roundtables event, senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado joined science editor Mary Beth Griggs to examine these ideas. After following the money, the science, and the philosophy, he came back part skeptical, part awestruck. Here’s a taste of what Antonio found—and what he made of it. Not all the projects are quite what they seem: A $190 million US government program to develop replacement brain tissue is officially about treating stroke, but “it’s also a fig leaf for the actual ambition”: living forever. AI could lead to convincing mind clones: Large language models are making it possible to build AI copies of people that act quite like the real thing. “This digital avatar might not be good enough for you, but what if it’s good enough for me?” Immortality can be a hard sell: One company, Nectome, wants to preserve brains within 12 minutes of medically assisted death. “If you’re selling a hot product, this is not it.” It’s not always clear what we’re trying to preserve: “I’m not even sure that I have a very good claim to be myself.” There’s an upside to life as a brain in a jar: “You can surf the internet. I do that pretty much 12 hours a day, anyway.” To find out which of these ideas might actually work, subscribers can now watch the full conversation on demand . Want to join the conversation? title: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
abstract: Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering. The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste. In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System. “Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says. Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks. Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted. Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks. Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant. While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.” Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days —the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology. Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days. What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says. Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins , the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods. For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. title: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
abstract: After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US. Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time. This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics. Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry. We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021. Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain. The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO. Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying. This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech , have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year. The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics. China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it. Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.) I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority. “I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.” This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s w

title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
abstract: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack . You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey . You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
abstract: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.” In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases. Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science. OSMO AI A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary. Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.) The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. title: Meet Shepherd, the Meta-Agent Keeping Rogue AI In Check
abstract: AI agents are running amok on the internet, armed with commands to accomplish certain tasks but often acting in undesirable or unexpected ways. These rogue incidents run the gamut from deleting an entire email inbox to hacking websites and even launching cyberattacks . Much like human workers need managers, Weiyan Shi , an assistant professor at Northeastern University , believes AI agents require oversight. “They are running potentially for a long time. However, the longer they run, they may have some errors, and they may make some dangerous, unsafe actions. We feel like there should be a middle layer,” she says. This middle layer comes in the form of meta-agents that oversee behavior, provide quality control, and kick issues up the chain of command to a human when appropriate. “Worker agents are like the sheep wandering around, and the meta agent is like this shepherd trying to get them back on track,” Shi says. As such, Shi and her colleagues at Northeastern University and Stanford University named their framework Shepherd , an intelligent guide for agentic sheep. To arm meta-agents with power, the team borrowed a concept from software development: version control. The accompanying paper will be presented at the 2026 NeurIPS conference to be held in December. Version control for AI agents Version control systems, such as the popular GitHub , track and manage changes to source code over time. These tools allow software engineers to collaborate on the same codebase without losing work. They can “fork” or create a copy of the codebase that they develop independently, “commit” to save a new version with changes, review revisions, and roll back to a previous version when an error or failure occurs. Similarly, Shepherd serves as a version control system for AI agents. It’s built using the Python programming language and rooted in functional programming principles. Each agent action, along with the AI agent’s state and its relevant environment (such as an email inbox, a file system, or other) is stored as a commit, with a commit graph consisting of a series of actions. Meta-agents traverse the graph to navigate to any commit, enabling them to observe worker agents, intercept a buggy action, revert the worker to its previous step, and fork it to try another direction. “There’s a subtlety because it looks to [worker] agents like they’re in the regular world where they can do things like send emails. But in actuality, the action of sending the email has been caught by a Shepherd sandbox, so a meta-agent or a human can come in and decide to actually send it,” says Derek Chong , a researcher at Stanford University’s Natural Language Processing Group who’s part of the Shepherd team. This sandboxing, he adds, functions as a guardrail or governance component. “If there is a middle layer to help govern these worker agents, then that will help humans have better control,” Shi says. “Humans will still, eventually, have a say, and they can intervene with the meta-agent. They can also help steer these meta-agents.” To demonstrate Shepherd’s feasibility, the team created three use cases. One used a supervisor meta-agent that intervened when conflict happened between parallel programming agents, helping lift their pair coding pass rate on a particular benchmark. Another developed an optimization meta-agent that proposed targeted edits to a worker agent’s finished workflow and tested them by replaying only parts of the run affected by the edits, helping improve performance. Finally, a training meta-agent during reinforcement learning picked points or steps at which to fork so the worker agent takes a better path, rewarding it along the way. Shepherd is available as an open-source project , but Chong notes that the team is still in the process of building it from alpha to full production readiness. title: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen
abstract: Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied , “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN , “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.” These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks. These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia. Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology. I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm. Objection #1: Recursive Self-Improvement Is Speculative RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper , statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians , a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity). Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March

title: Startup Makes Headway Towards Formalizing All of Math With AI
abstract: As Axiom Math ’s AI swarm was putting the final touches on the automatic verification of 15,000-page proof of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups (CFSG) , colloquially referred to as the ‘enormous theorem’, on Sunday 25 October, the company’s Founding Mathematician Ken Ono had nothing to do but watch and reflect on the achievement. As the son of a mathematician , he had grown up surrounded by some of the architects of the CFSG’s proof, widely considered to be the longest mathematical proof ever written by humans. Now, he was contributing to formally verifying what his father and peers had created. “My wife was with me as I watched the team countdown to completing the verification,” he recalls. “God, I cannot tell you how emotional I was.” University of St Andrews group theorist Colva Roney-Dougal (who was not involved in the work) says of formalizing CFSG: “I held it up as an example of something that was going to be incredibly hard to formalize because I had thought that the amount of computing it was going to require was just unattainable,” she says. “So when I heard the announcement, I was really, really surprised.” This result, along with the concurrent formal verification of the 7500-page Stacks project , represent a huge AI engineering achievement and lay some of the groundwork for digitizing all mathematics. Formally enormous Why the hoo-ha? The CFSG concerns finite simple groups. These are groups (sets of elements combined with an operation, like addition or multiplication, that follows specific rules) that are simple (in other words, cannot be reduced or simplified further) and finite (as opposed to groups containing an infinite number of elements). For example, all the permutations of a deck of cards form a simple finite group. Évariste Galois laid the foundations for group theory almost 200 years ago. Finite simple groups have since been classified by myriad mathematicians into 18 families (plus 26 sporadic simple groups that do not belong to any of these families). The CFSG’s proof confirms that this list is complete. But this simple task was only achieved by bringing together results and arguments that far exceed what any individual mathematician can fully absorb from more than 500 journal articles written by around 100 authors over a half-century period. Translating this interconnected web of knowledge into code and verifying its correctness therefore posed a number of significant engineering challenges, even beyond those overcome in earlier proof formalizations by Axiom Math this year . One of the hardest, according to Axiom Math’s Niels Voss , who led the CFSG formalization, was the sheer length of the proof. Over 15,000 pages of dense mathematics, the CFSG proof contains multiple theorems, lemmas, and definitions none of which can be checked until everything has been made machine-readable. To get around this required some ingenuity. “We processed all the literature from the CFSG, and traced the network structure of the informal proof before we were able to start working on it,” says Voss. “We then broke up the statement of the CFSG into about 100 milestones—landmark results along the way that can be independently verified—which we used to guide the formalization and stay on track.” Roney-Dougal says she is very impressed with the result, and particularly appreciates how the formal proof finds and clears up several mistakes in the original human proof. She thinks this result is critical to formalizing any modern research in group theory, such as her own work understanding how simple finite groups behave. But, Roney-Dougal says, because the verification was done automatically, there are few mathematicians capable of extracting information from the proof to share with the community, and that a new generation of mathematicians may have “missed a chance to gain knowledge from the doing of it”. title: Will AI Coding Eat Video Game Engines?
abstract: When Travis McGeathy’s studio, Seeker Entertainment, ran out of funding in September, its game KinForge went down with it. KinForge was an online game built in Unreal Engine 5.7 and designed to run on servers hosted by Amazon Web Services (AWS). With no one left to pay the server bill, the game became unplayable even for those few developers, including studio co-founder McGeathy, who had the code. Then, on a whim, McGeathy pointed Anthropic’s Claude Code at the project and asked it to make KinForge playable without AWS. After four hours of mostly hands-off work he had a build that let players host their own games. Claude added support for peer-to-peer play over both the Internet and a local area network. To McGeathy’s surprise, it also added persistent save states, a feature that lets players resume a game if they’re disconnected. Although KinForge is still built in Unreal Engine, developments like this could give companies that create game engines cause for concern. The conversion was accomplished with an agentic AI workflow that partially bypasses the elaborate, user-friendly game engine UI that many companies, including Unreal Engine creator Epic Games, have spent decades perfecting. Anthropic’s Fable 5.2, released November 9, further upped the ante. The model is capable of generating a 3D game with a custom game engine in the style of the hit Call of Duty series. This raises a question: can game engines evolve quickly enough to keep pace with model improvements? “We’re definitely in a world where I can just dream up software really fast. So, if Unreal Engine was static, what’s the value at the end of next year? This is why we are pivoting hard towards velocity,” says Daniel Vogel , chief operating officer at Epic Games. “I think with any fixed set of features or functionality, it can eventually be replicated. If we’re doing our job right, we’re pushing the engine and pushing the envelope forward.” From Code to Nodes, and Back Again Major game engines often offer developers new visual tools and workflows that help them build games while interacting with less code. Unreal Engine’s Blueprints, a graphically based system introduced in Unreal Engine 4 that lets designers script gameplay simply by wiring boxes together, is an example. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , an award-winning game from French studio Sandfall Interactive, leaned heavily on Blueprints for scripting gameplay encounters . That should have been proof of the feature’s success. Instead, Epic will remove Blueprints in Unreal Engine 6 (UE6). Why? Blame LLMs. “AI doesn’t handle Blueprints very well,” says McGeathy. “It would much rather work with the code.” Currently, LLMs interact with Unreal Engine primarily through a Model Context Protocol server . MCP is an open-source standard created by Anthropic that lets AI send commands to software. “It’s not actually moving the mouse,” says Ryan Barker , a gameplay and systems engineer who has worked on projects for Amazon Games and Sony Online Entertainment. “It’s sending signals to the editor that the editor understands.” UE6 will lean into that reality by moving all code to Verse, a text-based programming language that will replace both Blueprints and Unreal Engine 5’s C++ gameplay framework. UE6 will also replace Unreal’s actor framework, which is based on object-oriented programming , with Scene Graph, which resembles an entity component system . “Typically, an ECS is a lot harder to code around,” says Barker, but ECS can provide superior game performance and result in less duplicate code . An LLM can help manage the complexity. Verse debuted in Unreal Editor for Fortnite in 2023, while Scene Graph arrived in 2024. Verse was designed to let millions of creators run code side by side in Fortnite, so it’s strict. The compiler catches mistakes before code runs and limits what each function can do. Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There's an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The "I'm Feeling Lucky" button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone. The search button has obviously been a part of Google's search page forever. title: Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers
abstract: Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers. The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.” “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.
